## Sports injury treatment in Hyderabad, without surgery

Examined and scanned by ultrasound in one appointment at Kukatpally — and, if a procedure is right, treated there and then under local anaesthetic.

Book an appointment
Common questions

Most sports injuries are damage to a tendon, ligament or muscle, from a sudden strain or from overuse. At Halcyon the injury is scanned with ultrasound to grade the damage, then treated with regenerative therapy or prolotherapy so the tissue heals rather than just quietens down. Treatment is done under local anaesthetic as day care, and your return to sport is planned with you.

### What is a sports injury?

A sports injury is damage to the body’s soft tissues or joints caused by exercise or sport. Some happen in a moment — a twisted ankle, a pulled hamstring. Others build up over weeks of repeated load, such as a sore Achilles in a runner or an aching elbow in a racquet player.
You do not need to be an athlete to have one. Gym training, weekend cricket, badminton and walking programmes all produce the same kinds of tendon and ligament problems.

### Common causes of sports injuries

Sports injuries usually come from either a sudden overload or repeated stress that outpaces the tissue’s ability to recover. Typical examples include:
- Tendon overuse — Achilles, patellar, rotator cuff and elbow tendons
- Ligament sprains, most often at the ankle and knee
- Muscle strains, such as hamstring or calf tears
- Increasing training load too quickly, or too little recovery between sessions
- Poor technique, unsuitable footwear or an earlier injury that never fully healed

### Symptoms of a sports injury

A sudden injury usually causes immediate pain, swelling and sometimes bruising. Overuse injuries tend to creep up: pain that starts after training, then during it, then on everyday activity. Tendon problems are often stiff and sore first thing in the morning and ease once warmed up.
Other signs include tenderness over one spot, weakness, reduced movement, or a joint that feels unstable or gives way.

### How Halcyon finds the cause

The consultant examines the injured area and asks how it happened and how it has behaved since. The tendon, ligament or muscle is then scanned with diagnostic ultrasound in the same room. The scan shows whether the tissue is inflamed, partly torn or thickened from long-term overuse, and grades how much damage there is.
That grading decides the plan. A mildly overloaded tendon needs something different from a partial tear, and the scan also shows the consultant exactly where to place any injection.

### Non-surgical treatment options at Halcyon

Sports injuries at Halcyon are usually treated with regenerative therapy or prolotherapy, placed under ultrasound. Both aim to help the tissue repair rather than simply dull the pain.
Which one you are offered depends on what the scan shows. Treatment normally sits alongside a graded rehabilitation and loading programme, because a healed tendon or ligament still needs to be built back up before it takes full sporting load.
- Regenerative medicine — a growth factor concentrate prepared from a small sample of your own blood, placed where the tissue has worn or torn
- Prolotherapy — a natural irritant injected into a slack ligament or tendon to restart the body’s repair response, usually as a short course of small injections

### What to expect on the day and after

The examination, scan and procedure can all happen in one appointment at our Kukatpally centre. You stay awake under local anaesthetic, there is no admission, and most people are home within about two hours. Some soreness for a day or two after an injection is normal.
Return-to-sport timing is planned with you rather than handed to you. It depends on the tissue involved, the grade of injury and how it responds, and you will leave with aftercare instructions and a review date.

### When to see a doctor

Book an assessment if pain lasts more than two or three weeks, keeps returning when you train, or stops you playing. Some injuries need emergency care rather than a clinic visit.
- A visible deformity, or you cannot bear weight or use the limb — possible fracture or dislocation
- A head injury with confusion, vomiting or loss of consciousness
- Numbness, pins and needles or a cold, pale limb after an injury
- Severe swelling that develops quickly, or fever with a hot, swollen joint

### Treatments used for sports injuries

Which one is right is decided by what the scan shows, not chosen in advance.

Regenerative Medicine Regenerative medicine at Halcyon means a growth factor concentrate made from a small sample of your own blood and placed under ultrasound exactly where a tendon, ligament or joint has worn or torn. Prolotherapy Prolotherapy is an injection treatment in which a natural irritant is placed into a slack or weakened ligament or tendon to restart the body’s own repair response.

### Questions about sports injuries

**Can a sports injury be treated without surgery?**

Most tendon, ligament and overuse injuries can be. At Halcyon the injury is scanned to grade the damage and then treated with regenerative therapy or prolotherapy under ultrasound, under local anaesthetic as day care. Some injuries, such as a complete rupture or an unstable fracture, may need a surgical opinion, and you will be told that plainly.

**What is the difference between regenerative therapy and prolotherapy?**

Regenerative therapy uses a growth factor concentrate made from a small sample of your own blood, placed where tissue has worn or torn. Prolotherapy injects a natural irritant into a slack ligament or tendon to restart the body’s repair response. The scan decides which suits your injury.

**When can I return to sport?**

It depends on the tissue involved, how badly it is damaged and how it responds to treatment. Your consultant plans the return with you, usually alongside a graded loading programme, so that the tissue is strong enough for full training before you go back to it.

**Do I need an MRI before coming in?**

Not necessarily. Many tendon, ligament and muscle injuries can be assessed with diagnostic ultrasound during the consultation. If you already have an X-ray or MRI, bring the report — it often saves a second visit. The consultant will tell you if further imaging is needed.

**Will the injection hurt?**

The procedure is done under local anaesthetic, so you stay awake and talking but the area is numbed. Some soreness at the injection site for a day or two afterwards is normal, particularly after prolotherapy. The consultant will explain what to expect and how to manage it.

**How do I book a sports injury assessment in Hyderabad?**

Call Halcyon on +91 77880 91092, Monday to Saturday, 9 am to 6 pm. The centre is at Kukatpally Y Junction, above the Max showroom on Moosapet Road. Bring any scan reports and details of earlier treatment for the injury. Costs are explained at the consultation, before anything is booked.

Usual procedure Regenerative injection or prolotherapy

Anaesthesia Local anaesthetic — awake throughout

Hospital stay None — day care, home the same day

Return to sport Planned with you, based on the injury

## Trigeminal neuralgia treatment in Hyderabad

Examined and scanned by ultrasound in one appointment at Kukatpally — and, if a procedure is right, treated there and then under local anaesthetic.

Book an appointment
Common questions

Trigeminal neuralgia causes sudden, electric-shock-like pain across one side of the face, usually set off by light touch, chewing or talking. Medication is the usual first treatment; when it no longer controls the pain, Halcyon offers image-guided radiofrequency ablation of the affected branch of the nerve, under local anaesthetic as day care. It is worth being assessed early, because trigeminal neuralgia rarely settles on its own.

### What is trigeminal neuralgia?

Trigeminal neuralgia is a long-term nerve pain condition affecting the trigeminal nerve, which carries sensation from the face. It causes brief attacks of severe, shooting pain — often described as an electric shock — in the area supplied by one or more of the nerve’s three branches.
The first branch supplies the forehead and eye, the second the cheek and upper lip, and the third the jaw, lower lip and teeth. It usually affects one side of the face.

### Common causes of trigeminal neuralgia

In many people the cause is a blood vessel pressing on the trigeminal nerve close to where it leaves the brainstem, which wears away the nerve’s protective coating. Sometimes no cause is found. Less often it is secondary to another condition:
- Pressure on the nerve from a nearby blood vessel
- Multiple sclerosis
- A tumour or cyst pressing on the nerve
- Injury to the nerve from facial trauma or surgery, including dental surgery

### Symptoms of trigeminal neuralgia

The typical pattern is sudden stabbing or shock-like pain lasting from a fraction of a second to about two minutes, sometimes in rapid bursts. Between attacks there may be no pain at all, though some people have a background ache or burning.
Attacks are often triggered by everyday things: washing or touching the face, shaving, brushing teeth, chewing, talking, or a cold breeze. Many people first see a dentist, because the pain can feel as if it comes from a tooth.

### How Halcyon finds the cause

The diagnosis is mostly made from the pattern of your pain and a careful examination of the face to work out which branch of the nerve is involved. An MRI of the brain is commonly advised to look for a blood vessel or another cause pressing on the nerve. Bring any earlier MRI reports and a list of the medicines you have tried, with doses.
Before any radiofrequency treatment, the consultant needs to be confident that the branch being treated is the one carrying the pain. The plan is built around that confirmation rather than around a guess.

### Non-surgical treatment options at Halcyon

Medication, usually an anticonvulsant prescribed and adjusted by your doctor, is the standard first treatment and works well for many people. Over time some find it stops controlling the pain or causes side effects they cannot live with.
At that point Halcyon offers radiofrequency ablation of the affected branch. A precise current, delivered through a fine needle under image guidance, interrupts the nerve fibres carrying the pain signal. It aims for longer-lasting relief without open surgery. How long relief lasts varies from person to person, and the procedure can be repeated if the pain returns. Some numbness in the treated area afterwards is a known effect, and the consultant will discuss this with you beforehand.

### What to expect on the day and after

The procedure is done under local anaesthetic, so you stay awake and can talk to the consultant throughout. There is no general anaesthetic and no admission; most people are home within about two hours.
You will leave with aftercare instructions and a review date. Do not stop or change your medication on your own — any reduction is planned with your doctor once the effect of treatment is clear.

### When to see a doctor

See a doctor if you have repeated attacks of sharp facial pain, especially if dental treatment has not explained them. Some facial symptoms need urgent assessment instead of a clinic appointment.
- Sudden facial drooping, slurred speech, or weakness of an arm or leg — go to an emergency department now
- Facial pain with loss of vision, double vision or a severe new headache
- Numbness of the face that is spreading or persistent
- Facial pain with fever, or swelling of the face or jaw

### Treatments used for trigeminal neuralgia

Which one is right is decided by what the scan shows, not chosen in advance.

Radiofrequency Ablation Radiofrequency ablation uses a precise, controlled current to interrupt the nerve that carries a pain signal.

### Questions about trigeminal neuralgia

**Can trigeminal neuralgia be treated without surgery?**

Yes, for many people. Medication is the usual first step. When it no longer controls the pain, Halcyon offers radiofrequency ablation of the affected branch of the trigeminal nerve — an image-guided needle procedure under local anaesthetic, done as day care, with no open surgery and no hospital admission.

**Does trigeminal neuralgia go away on its own?**

It rarely settles on its own. Some people have pain-free spells lasting weeks or months, but attacks usually return and can become more frequent over time. That is why it is worth being assessed early, rather than waiting for the pain to stop by itself.

**What does radiofrequency ablation do for facial pain?**

A fine needle is guided to the affected branch of the trigeminal nerve and a precise current interrupts the fibres carrying the pain signal. It is offered when medication has stopped working or causes too many side effects. How long relief lasts varies, and the procedure can be repeated if needed.

**Will my face feel numb afterwards?**

Some numbness or altered sensation in the area supplied by the treated branch is a known effect of radiofrequency treatment. How much varies from person to person. The consultant will explain the likely effects for your case before you decide, so you can weigh them against the pain.

**Can I stop my medicines after the procedure?**

Not on your own. Anticonvulsants used for trigeminal neuralgia should be reduced gradually and only on medical advice. Once the effect of the procedure is clear, any change to your medication is planned with your doctor. Tell the team about every medicine you take, especially blood thinners, when you book.

**How do I book an assessment in Hyderabad?**

Call Halcyon on +91 77880 91092, Monday to Saturday, 9 am to 6 pm. The centre is at Kukatpally Y Junction, above the Max showroom on Moosapet Road. Bring any MRI reports and a list of the medicines you have tried. Costs are given at the consultation, before anything is booked.

Usual procedure Radiofrequency ablation of the affected branch

Anaesthesia Local anaesthetic — awake throughout

Hospital stay None — day care, home the same day

Surgery Not part of treatment at Halcyon

## Elbow, hand and wrist pain treatment in Hyderabad, without surgery

Examined and scanned by ultrasound in one appointment at Kukatpally — and, if a procedure is right, treated there and then under local anaesthetic.

Book an appointment
Common questions

Most elbow, hand and wrist pain comes from an overloaded tendon, such as tennis elbow or de Quervain’s, or a trapped nerve, as in carpal tunnel syndrome. At Halcyon these are usually treated with ultrasound-guided nerve hydrodissection or a regenerative injection — freeing or repairing the structure rather than releasing it surgically. Treatment is under local anaesthetic, as day care.

### What is elbow, hand and wrist pain?

Elbow, hand and wrist pain covers a group of problems in the forearm and hand, most of them from tendons that have been overloaded by repeated gripping and twisting, or from a nerve squeezed as it passes through a narrow space.
The three seen most often at Halcyon are tennis elbow, carpal tunnel syndrome and de Quervain’s tenosynovitis. They can make ordinary tasks — lifting a cup, typing, opening a jar, holding a phone — surprisingly painful.

### Common causes of elbow, hand and wrist pain

Repetitive use is the common thread. The main conditions are:
- Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) — overload and small tears in the forearm tendons where they attach to the outer elbow
- Golfer’s elbow — the same process on the inner side of the elbow
- Carpal tunnel syndrome — the median nerve compressed as it passes through the wrist
- De Quervain’s tenosynovitis — irritation of the tendons at the base of the thumb, common in new parents and heavy phone or keyboard users
- Pain referred from the neck, which should be ruled out when there is tingling in the hand

### Symptoms of elbow, hand and wrist pain

Tennis elbow causes pain on the outer elbow that can spread into the forearm, worse with gripping, shaking hands or turning a bottle cap. De Quervain’s causes pain on the thumb side of the wrist, especially when gripping or lifting with the thumb.
Carpal tunnel syndrome is different: numbness, tingling or burning in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often worse at night or on waking, with clumsiness or a weaker grip as it progresses.

### How Halcyon finds the cause

The consultant examines the elbow, wrist and hand, and checks the neck if there is tingling, because a nerve root irritated in the neck can mimic a problem at the wrist. The tendon or nerve is then scanned with diagnostic ultrasound in the same room.
Ultrasound shows a thickened or torn tendon, fluid around a tendon sheath, or a swollen median nerve at the wrist. The same scan then guides the needle, so the treatment reaches the structure that is actually causing the pain.

### Non-surgical treatment options at Halcyon

Elbow, hand and wrist pain at Halcyon is usually treated with nerve hydrodissection or a regenerative injection, chosen by what the scan shows. The aim is to free a trapped nerve or help a worn tendon repair, rather than release it surgically.
- Nerve hydrodissection — for a trapped nerve such as in carpal tunnel syndrome. Fluid is placed under ultrasound to separate the nerve from the tissue pressing on it. Relief often begins on the table, and the nerve itself is left intact.
- Regenerative injection — for a worn or partly torn tendon, such as in tennis elbow. A growth factor concentrate made from a small sample of your own blood is placed under ultrasound where the tendon has worn.
- Nerve block — used where needed to quieten a nerve that is firing, or to confirm where the pain is coming from.

### What to expect on the day and after

The examination, scan and procedure can all happen in one appointment at the Kukatpally centre. You stay awake under local anaesthetic, with no admission, and most people are home within about two hours.
You will leave with aftercare instructions, advice on which activities to ease off for a while, and a review date. Costs are explained at the consultation, before anything is booked.

### When to see a doctor

Book an assessment if pain or tingling lasts more than a few weeks, wakes you at night, or you start dropping things. Some symptoms need urgent care instead of a clinic visit.
- A fall onto the hand or elbow followed by swelling, deformity or inability to move it — possible fracture
- A hot, red, swollen joint or finger, especially with fever — possible infection
- Sudden weakness of the hand or arm, or weakness with facial drooping or slurred speech — go to an emergency department now
- Numbness that is getting steadily worse, or wasting of the muscles at the base of the thumb

### Treatments used for elbow, hand & wrist

Which one is right is decided by what the scan shows, not chosen in advance.

Nerve Hydrodissection & Nerve Blocks Nerve hydrodissection uses fluid, placed under ultrasound, to separate a trapped nerve from the tissue pressing on it, leaving the nerve itself intact. Regenerative Medicine Regenerative medicine at Halcyon means a growth factor concentrate made from a small sample of your own blood and placed under ultrasound exactly where a tendon, ligament or joint has worn or torn.

### Questions about elbow, hand & wrist

**Can carpal tunnel syndrome be treated without surgery?**

Often, yes. At Halcyon carpal tunnel syndrome is usually treated with ultrasound-guided nerve hydrodissection: fluid is placed around the median nerve to separate it from the tissue pressing on it. Relief often begins on the table, and the nerve is left intact. It is done under local anaesthetic as day care.

**What is the treatment for tennis elbow?**

Tennis elbow is an overloaded, often partly torn, tendon on the outer elbow. At Halcyon it is usually treated with a regenerative injection — growth factor concentrate from your own blood, placed under ultrasound where the tendon has worn — alongside advice on easing the load while it repairs.

**What is nerve hydrodissection?**

It is a procedure in which fluid is injected under ultrasound guidance to separate a trapped nerve from the tissue pressing on it. Nothing is cut and the nerve itself is left intact. Many people notice relief beginning on the table, though how much and how long varies from person to person.

**What is de Quervain’s tenosynovitis?**

It is irritation of two tendons that run along the thumb side of the wrist, causing pain when you grip, pinch or lift with the thumb. It is common in new parents and in people who use a phone or keyboard heavily. Ultrasound shows the tendon sheath and guides treatment to it.

**Why does the consultant check my neck for hand tingling?**

A nerve root irritated in the neck can cause tingling in the hand that feels just like carpal tunnel syndrome, and sometimes both are present. Examining the neck as well as the wrist makes sure the right source is treated. Bring any earlier nerve conduction or MRI reports.

**How do I book an appointment in Hyderabad?**

Call Halcyon on +91 77880 91092, Monday to Saturday, 9 am to 6 pm. The centre is at Kukatpally Y Junction, above the Max showroom on Moosapet Road. Bring any scan or nerve study reports, a list of your medicines and notes from earlier treatment.

## Foot and ankle pain treatment in Hyderabad, without surgery

Examined and scanned by ultrasound in one appointment at Kukatpally — and, if a procedure is right, treated there and then under local anaesthetic.

Book an appointment
Common questions

Heel pain that is worst on the first steps of the morning is usually plantar fasciitis; pain at the back of the ankle is often Achilles tendinitis. At Halcyon both are scanned with ultrasound and usually treated with prolotherapy or a regenerative injection placed under ultrasound guidance. Treatment is under local anaesthetic as day care, and you walk out the same day.

### What is foot and ankle pain?

Foot and ankle pain is pain in the heel, the sole, the arch or around the ankle. The two commonest causes seen at Halcyon are plantar fasciitis — irritation and thickening of the band of tissue under the foot that supports the arch — and Achilles tendinitis, which affects the large tendon joining the calf to the heel.
Both are usually overuse problems, and both tend to linger for months if the tissue is not given a reason to repair.

### Common causes of foot and ankle pain

Foot and ankle pain usually comes from repeated load on the plantar fascia or Achilles tendon, more than the tissue can recover from. Common contributors include:
- Long hours standing or walking, especially on hard floors
- Running, jumping or a sudden increase in activity
- Footwear with little support or cushioning
- Flat feet, high arches or tight calf muscles
- Increased body weight, which adds load to the heel
- An old ankle sprain that left the ligaments slack

### Symptoms of foot and ankle pain

Plantar fasciitis typically causes a sharp or stabbing pain under the heel on the first steps out of bed, or after sitting for a while, which eases a little as you move and returns after long periods on your feet.
Achilles tendinitis causes pain and stiffness at the back of the heel or just above it, often worse in the morning and after activity, sometimes with swelling or a tender thickening of the tendon. Standing on tiptoe or climbing stairs may hurt.

### How Halcyon finds the cause

The consultant examines the foot and ankle, watches how you stand and walk, and asks about your work, activity and footwear. The plantar fascia or Achilles tendon is then scanned with diagnostic ultrasound in the same room.
The scan shows how thickened or torn the tissue is and rules out other causes of heel pain. It is then used to guide the needle to the exact point that needs treating.

### Non-surgical treatment options at Halcyon

Plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendinitis at Halcyon usually respond to prolotherapy or a regenerative injection placed under ultrasound. Both aim to help the tissue repair and hold again, rather than simply quieten the pain.
Which you are offered depends on the scan. Treatment usually goes alongside stretching, loading exercises and footwear advice, so the repaired tissue is not overloaded again straight away.
- Prolotherapy — a natural irritant injected into a slack ligament or tendon to restart the body’s repair response, given as a short course of small injections with minimal downtime
- Regenerative medicine — a growth factor concentrate prepared from a small sample of your own blood, placed where the tissue has worn

### What to expect on the day and after

The examination, scan and procedure can all happen in one appointment at our Kukatpally centre. You stay awake under local anaesthetic, there is no admission, and most people are home within about two hours.
Some soreness for a day or two after prolotherapy is normal. You will leave with aftercare instructions, advice on activity and footwear, and a review date. Costs are explained at the consultation, before anything is booked.

### When to see a doctor

See a doctor if heel or ankle pain lasts more than a few weeks or keeps you from walking comfortably. Some foot symptoms need urgent attention instead of a clinic visit.
- A sudden snap or pop at the back of the ankle with difficulty pushing off — possible Achilles rupture, go to an emergency department
- Unable to bear weight after a fall or twist — possible fracture
- A hot, red, swollen foot, especially with fever
- A wound, ulcer or colour change on the foot if you have diabetes
- Numbness or burning in both feet that is spreading

### Treatments used for foot & ankle pain

Which one is right is decided by what the scan shows, not chosen in advance.

Prolotherapy Prolotherapy is an injection treatment in which a natural irritant is placed into a slack or weakened ligament or tendon to restart the body’s own repair response. Regenerative Medicine Regenerative medicine at Halcyon means a growth factor concentrate made from a small sample of your own blood and placed under ultrasound exactly where a tendon, ligament or joint has worn or torn.

### Questions about foot & ankle pain

**Can plantar fasciitis be treated without surgery?**

Usually, yes. At Halcyon plantar fasciitis is scanned with ultrasound and then commonly treated with prolotherapy or a regenerative injection placed under ultrasound guidance, alongside stretching and footwear advice. The procedure is done under local anaesthetic as day care, and you walk out the same day.

**Why is my heel pain worst in the morning?**

Overnight the plantar fascia tightens while you rest. The first steps stretch it suddenly, which is why heel pain from plantar fasciitis is typically sharpest when you get out of bed, and again after sitting for a while. It often eases a little once you have been moving.

**What is prolotherapy for the heel or Achilles?**

Prolotherapy is an injection of a natural irritant into a slack or overused ligament or tendon to restart the body’s own repair response. It is given as a short course of small injections under ultrasound, with minimal downtime. Some soreness for a day or two afterwards is normal.

**How is Achilles tendinitis different from a torn Achilles?**

Achilles tendinitis builds up gradually, with pain and stiffness at the back of the heel. A rupture usually happens suddenly, with a snap or a feeling of being kicked, and difficulty pushing off the foot. A suspected rupture needs urgent assessment at a hospital rather than a clinic appointment.

**Will I be able to walk after the injection?**

Yes. You walk out after the procedure and most people go about a normal day. The consultant will tell you how much to ease off standing, running or sport while the tissue repairs, and what footwear or exercises will help before you leave.

## Cervical spondylosis treatment in Hyderabad, without surgery

Examined and scanned by ultrasound in one appointment at Kukatpally — and, if a procedure is right, treated there and then under local anaesthetic.

Book an appointment
Common questions

Cervical spondylosis is age-related wear of the discs and facet joints in the neck. The wear shows on almost every scan after a certain age, so at Halcyon a medial branch block is used first to prove that the worn facet joints are what is actually hurting. If the block confirms it, cervical facet radiofrequency treats them — under local anaesthetic, as day care.

### What is cervical spondylosis?

Cervical spondylosis is the general term for wear and tear in the neck — discs that lose height and water, facet joints that develop arthritis, and small bony spurs at the edges of the vertebrae. It becomes more common with age, and many people with these changes on a scan have no pain at all.
When it does hurt, the pain usually comes from specific structures: most often the facet joints at the back of the neck, sometimes a disc or a nerve root narrowed by the wear.

### Common causes of cervical spondylosis

Ageing is the main cause, but some things add to the load on the neck and can make wear, or its symptoms, arrive earlier:
- Age-related drying and thinning of the neck discs
- Arthritis of the cervical facet joints
- Bone spurs that narrow the space for the nerve roots
- Long hours at a desk, laptop or phone with the head held forward
- An earlier neck injury, heavy overhead work, or smoking

### Symptoms of cervical spondylosis

The usual symptoms are neck pain and stiffness, often worse after holding one position and in the morning, with difficulty turning the head to reverse a car or look over your shoulder. Pain can spread to the shoulder blades or the back of the head and cause headaches.
If a nerve root is narrowed, you may feel pain, tingling or numbness running into the arm or hand. Less commonly the spinal cord itself is affected, which is covered under when to see a doctor below.

### How Halcyon finds the cause

Because the wear appears on almost every scan after a certain age, the scan alone does not make the diagnosis. The consultant examines your neck, shoulders and arms, checks reflexes and strength, and reviews any X-ray or MRI you bring.
If a facet joint is the likely source, a medial branch block is done first. A small amount of local anaesthetic is placed on the tiny nerves supplying that joint under image guidance. If your usual pain settles, that joint is confirmed as the source; if it does not, the plan changes. This is what stands between a diagnosis and a guess.

### Non-surgical treatment options at Halcyon

When the medial branch block confirms the worn facet joints are causing the pain, Halcyon treats them with cervical facet radiofrequency. A precise current, delivered through a fine needle under image guidance, interrupts the small nerves carrying pain from the joint. The joint itself is not operated on.
Radiofrequency is never the first thing done — it follows only a positive block. Where the scan and examination point to an irritated nerve root rather than a facet joint, a different image-guided injection aimed at that root may be advised instead. Posture changes and a neck exercise programme are usually part of the plan.

### What to expect on the day and after

Both the block and the radiofrequency procedure are done under local anaesthetic, so you stay awake and talking. There is no general anaesthetic and no admission, and most people are home within about two hours of their procedure at the Kukatpally centre.
You will leave with aftercare instructions and a review date, and the consultant will tell you what to do and what to avoid before you go. Costs are explained at the consultation, before anything is booked.

### When to see a doctor

See a doctor if neck pain lasts more than a few weeks or spreads into your arm. Signs that the spinal cord may be under pressure need urgent assessment in a hospital rather than a clinic appointment.
- Weakness in the arms or legs, or clumsy hands that are getting worse
- Unsteady walking or loss of balance
- Loss of bladder or bowel control
- Neck pain with fever, or after a fall or accident
- Neck pain with a severe sudden headache, or numbness spreading on both sides

### Treatments used for cervical spondylosis

Which one is right is decided by what the scan shows, not chosen in advance.

Radiofrequency Ablation Radiofrequency ablation uses a precise, controlled current to interrupt the nerve that carries a pain signal. Nerve Hydrodissection & Nerve Blocks Nerve hydrodissection uses fluid, placed under ultrasound, to separate a trapped nerve from the tissue pressing on it, leaving the nerve itself intact.

### Questions about cervical spondylosis

**Can cervical spondylosis be treated without surgery?**

In most cases, yes. At Halcyon a medial branch block is used first to prove whether the worn facet joints are causing your pain. If it confirms them, cervical facet radiofrequency treats them. Both are image-guided needle procedures under local anaesthetic, done as day care with no admission.

**My MRI shows spondylosis. Does that explain my pain?**

Not necessarily. Wear in the neck shows on almost every scan after a certain age, including in people with no pain. That is why the scan alone does not make the diagnosis at Halcyon. A medial branch block is used to prove which joint, if any, is actually causing your pain.

**What is a medial branch block?**

It is a small injection of local anaesthetic placed under image guidance on the tiny nerves that supply a facet joint. If your usual pain settles afterwards, that joint is confirmed as the source and radiofrequency can be considered. If the pain does not change, the plan changes instead of treating the wrong structure.

**What does cervical facet radiofrequency involve?**

A fine needle is guided to the small nerves carrying pain from the confirmed facet joint, and a precise current interrupts their signal. You stay awake under local anaesthetic and go home the same day. How long relief lasts varies, and the consultant will give you a realistic answer for your neck.

**Can cervical spondylosis cause arm pain or tingling?**

Yes. If the wear narrows the space where a nerve root leaves the spine, you may feel pain, tingling or numbness running into the arm or hand. Weakness that is getting worse, clumsy hands or unsteady walking need urgent assessment, because they can mean the spinal cord is under pressure.

**How do I book an appointment in Hyderabad?**

Call Halcyon on +91 77880 91092, Monday to Saturday, 9 am to 6 pm. The centre is at Kukatpally Y Junction, above the Max showroom on Moosapet Road. Bring your X-ray or MRI reports and a list of your medicines — tell the team if you take blood thinners.

## Regenerative medicine in Hyderabad, from your own blood

Image-guided, under local anaesthetic, as day care — and chosen by what the diagnostic scan shows, not from a menu.

Book an appointment
Common questions

Regenerative medicine at Halcyon means a growth factor concentrate made from a small sample of your own blood and placed under ultrasound exactly where a tendon, ligament or joint has worn or torn. It aims to prompt the body to repair the tissue rather than to mask the pain. It is done as day care under local anaesthetic, and you go home the same day.

### What is regenerative medicine?

Regenerative medicine is a non-surgical injection treatment that uses a concentrate of growth factors taken from your own blood to support the repair of damaged tissue. At Halcyon in Hyderabad it is known as growth factor concentrate, and it is always placed under ultrasound guidance.
Nothing foreign is introduced. The concentrate is prepared from a blood sample taken on the day, so the treatment relies on your body’s own healing signals rather than on a drug.

### How growth factor concentrate works

Growth factor concentrate works by delivering a high dose of the body’s own repair signals to a structure that has stopped healing well on its own. Blood contains platelets, and platelets carry growth factors that help organise tissue repair after an injury.
When a tendon or ligament has been overused, partly torn or slowly worn, the normal healing response often stalls. Concentrating those growth factors and placing them precisely in the damaged tissue is intended to restart that response. Because it works on repair rather than on the pain signal, it is used where a structure has worn or torn, not where a nerve is simply firing.

### Which conditions regenerative medicine helps

At Halcyon, regenerative medicine is most often used for knee, shoulder, hip, foot and ankle, and elbow, hand and wrist problems, and for sports injuries. The scan decides whether it is the right choice for your case.
- Knee pain from early to moderate osteoarthritis or ligament and meniscal problems
- Shoulder pain from rotator cuff tendon problems
- Hip pain involving the tendons or bursa around the hip, or an arthritic joint
- Sports injuries to tendons, ligaments and muscles
- Foot and ankle pain such as plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendinitis
- Elbow, hand and wrist pain such as tennis elbow and golfer’s elbow

### Who it suits, and who it does not

Regenerative medicine usually suits people whose pain comes from a tendon, ligament or joint that is worn or partly torn, and whose problem has not settled with rest, physiotherapy and simple painkillers. The diagnostic ultrasound at your consultation shows whether the tissue is the kind that can respond.
It is less suitable when the pain is mainly coming from an irritated nerve, where a nerve block or radiofrequency may fit better, and it is not a substitute for surgery in advanced grade 4 knee arthritis with joint deformity. If a replacement is the right answer, you will be told that plainly. An active infection, certain blood disorders or some medicines may also mean it is postponed or not advised.

### The procedure, step by step

The whole process usually takes place in a single appointment at the Kukatpally centre, and most people are home within about two hours of arriving.
- The consultant takes your history and examines the painful area.
- A diagnostic ultrasound is done in the same room to find the structure that is damaged.
- If regenerative medicine is right, a small sample of blood is drawn from your arm.
- The sample is processed to concentrate its growth factors.
- The skin is cleaned and numbed with local anaesthetic.
- Under live ultrasound, the concentrate is placed precisely into the damaged tissue.
- You rest briefly, receive aftercare instructions and a review date, and go home.

### Recovery and aftercare

Most people walk out after a regenerative injection and go about a light day, with some soreness or a feeling of fullness at the site for a few days. This is expected, because the treatment works by stirring up a repair response.
You will be told how much to use the area, when to restart exercise and whether any painkillers should be avoided, because some anti-inflammatory medicines may interfere with the healing response. Physiotherapy or a graded exercise programme is often part of the plan. Some people need more than one injection; the consultant will tell you whether a repeat is likely for your condition.

### Safety and side effects

Because the concentrate comes from your own blood, allergic reactions to it are not expected. The main side effects are those of any injection: pain, swelling or bruising at the site for a few days, and, rarely, infection.
Ultrasound guidance helps the needle reach the intended tissue and avoid nearby nerves and vessels. Contact the team if you develop increasing redness, heat, fever or pain that is getting worse rather than better, and seek urgent care if you feel unwell with a high temperature.

### Conditions it is used for

Each links to how that condition is assessed and treated at Halcyon.

- Knee Pain
- Shoulder Pain
- Hip Pain
- Sports Injuries
- Foot & Ankle Pain
- Elbow, Hand & Wrist

### Questions about regenerative medicine

**What is growth factor concentrate?**

Growth factor concentrate is a preparation made from a small sample of your own blood, processed so that the growth factors carried by platelets are concentrated. At Halcyon it is placed under ultrasound into a worn or torn tendon, ligament or joint to prompt the body’s own repair response. Nothing foreign is added, because it comes from a sample taken on the day.

**Is regenerative medicine the same as PRP?**

They are closely related. Both use platelets from your own blood, and both rely on the growth factors those platelets release. Halcyon uses a growth factor concentrate, placed under ultrasound guidance. The consultant can explain the preparation used in your case and why it suits the structure the scan has found.

**How long before a regenerative injection starts to work?**

Improvement is usually gradual rather than immediate, because the treatment works by supporting tissue repair rather than by numbing pain. Many people notice change over the following weeks, and the site can feel sore for the first few days. How much it helps, and for how long, depends on the condition and how worn the tissue is, which the consultant will discuss with you.

**Does a regenerative injection hurt?**

The skin is numbed with local anaesthetic first, and you stay awake throughout, so you can tell the consultant what you feel. Most people describe pressure rather than sharp pain during the injection. Soreness or a sense of fullness at the site for a few days afterwards is common and expected, and you will be told how to manage it.

**Can regenerative medicine help knee arthritis without surgery?**

For many people with early to moderate knee osteoarthritis, a regenerative injection is one of the non-surgical options, alongside cooled radiofrequency and prolotherapy. Which is right depends on what the scan shows. For advanced grade 4 arthritis with joint deformity, a replacement may still be the right answer, and the consultant will say so plainly rather than treat you anyway.

**How much does regenerative medicine cost at Halcyon?**

The cost depends on the area treated and how many sittings are needed, so the team gives you a clear figure at the consultation, before anything is booked. Insurance cover depends on your policy and the procedure; ask the team when you call +91 77880 91092 and they can tell you what applies and what paperwork you would need.

Title: Radiofrequency Ablation in Hyderabad | Halcyon

Treatments

## Radiofrequency ablation in Hyderabad, after the block confirms the source

Image-guided, under local anaesthetic, as day care — and chosen by what the diagnostic scan shows, not from a menu.

Book an appointment
Common questions

Radiofrequency ablation uses a precise, controlled current to interrupt the nerve that carries a pain signal. At Halcyon it is used for knee, neck, low back and trigeminal nerve pain, with the US FDA-cleared COOLIEF cooled RF system for the knee, and only after a diagnostic block has confirmed the source. It is done under local anaesthetic as day care, and you go home the same day.

### What is radiofrequency ablation?

Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is a non-surgical procedure in which a fine probe, placed through a needle under image guidance, delivers a controlled current to a small sensory nerve so that it stops carrying the pain signal. It treats the nerve that reports the pain, not the joint itself.
At Halcyon in Kukatpally, Hyderabad, radiofrequency is never the first thing done. A diagnostic block must first show that the nerve in question is the one carrying your pain.

### How radiofrequency ablation works

Radiofrequency ablation works by creating a small, controlled area of heat around the tip of the probe, which interrupts the sensory nerve’s ability to send pain signals to the brain. The nerves treated are small sensory branches, chosen so that the muscles you use to move are not affected.
For knee pain, Halcyon uses the US FDA-cleared COOLIEF cooled RF system. Its water-cooled probe treats a larger volume of tissue than standard radiofrequency, so the genicular nerves around the knee, whose paths vary from person to person, can be reached more completely. For the neck and low back, radiofrequency is applied to the medial branch nerves that supply the facet joints.

### Which conditions radiofrequency ablation helps

At Halcyon, radiofrequency ablation is most often used for five conditions, each after a block has confirmed the source.
- Knee pain, including osteoarthritis — COOLIEF cooled RF of the genicular nerves
- Neck pain from the facet joints — cervical facet radiofrequency after a medial branch block
- Cervical spondylosis, when a block proves the worn facet joints are what hurts
- Low back pain from the facet joints, once a diagnostic block has identified them
- Trigeminal neuralgia, when medication no longer controls the pain — radiofrequency of the affected branch

### Who it suits, and who it does not

Radiofrequency ablation usually suits people with long-standing joint or nerve pain whose diagnostic block gave clear relief, and who want to avoid or put off surgery. For the knee, it is often considered when pain continues despite medicines and physiotherapy.
It is not suitable when the block does not settle the pain, because that means the nerve tested is not the source and the plan changes. It will not correct a deformed joint: in advanced grade 4 knee arthritis with deformity, a replacement may still be the right answer, and you will be told so plainly. An active infection, some bleeding problems or uncontrolled medical conditions may also mean it is delayed or not advised.

### The procedure, step by step

The consultation, scan and diagnostic block come first. Radiofrequency follows only when the block confirms the source, and the consultant will tell you when it is scheduled.
- The consultant takes your history, examines you and scans the area with diagnostic ultrasound.
- A diagnostic block is placed on the suspected nerve to see whether the pain settles.
- If it does, the radiofrequency procedure is planned for that nerve.
- On the day, the skin is cleaned and numbed with local anaesthetic; you stay awake.
- Under image guidance, the probe is positioned beside the target nerve and its position is checked.
- A controlled current is applied, one nerve at a time.
- You rest briefly, receive aftercare instructions and a review date, and go home the same day.

### Recovery and aftercare

Most people walk out after radiofrequency ablation and can manage light activity the same day. Soreness at the needle sites, or a temporary flare of the usual pain, is common for a few days before the benefit becomes clear.
You will be told what to do and what to avoid before you leave. How long relief lasts varies with the condition and how worn the joint is. The treated nerve can regrow over time, and if the pain returns, the procedure can often be repeated; the consultant will give you a realistic answer for your case.

### Safety and side effects

Radiofrequency ablation is generally well tolerated. Common, usually short-lived effects include soreness, bruising and a patch of numbness or altered sensation over the treated area. Less often there can be temporary nerve irritation, and, rarely, infection or bleeding.
Image guidance and careful positioning of the probe keep the treatment to the intended sensory nerve. Tell the team about blood thinners when you book, and do not stop them on your own. Seek urgent care for fever, spreading redness, new weakness or pain that is rapidly getting worse.

### Conditions it is used for

Each links to how that condition is assessed and treated at Halcyon.

- Knee Pain
- Neck Pain
- Cervical Spondylosis
- Low Back Pain
- Trigeminal Neuralgia

### Questions about radiofrequency ablation

**What is COOLIEF cooled radiofrequency?**

COOLIEF is a US FDA-cleared cooled radiofrequency system, and it is what Halcyon uses for knee pain. A water-cooled probe allows the treatment to cover a larger volume of tissue than standard radiofrequency, so the genicular nerves that carry pain from the knee can be reached more completely. It is done under local anaesthetic as day care.

**Why is a diagnostic block done before radiofrequency?**

A diagnostic block is a small injection of local anaesthetic on the suspected nerve. If your pain settles afterwards, that nerve is carrying the pain and radiofrequency is likely to help. If it does not, the source lies elsewhere and the plan changes. At Halcyon, radiofrequency is never the first step; in the neck and low back this means a medial branch block first.

**Is radiofrequency ablation painful?**

The skin and deeper tissues are numbed with local anaesthetic, and you stay awake and able to talk to the consultant throughout. Most people feel pressure and some warmth or aching during the treatment rather than sharp pain. Soreness at the needle sites for a few days afterwards is common, and you will be told how to manage it.

**How long does relief from radiofrequency ablation last?**

It varies with the condition, how worn the joint is and what is causing the pain, which is why the diagnostic scan and block come first. The treated nerve can gradually regrow, and if the pain returns, the procedure can often be repeated. The consultant will give you a realistic answer for your case rather than a number that fits everyone.

**Can radiofrequency ablation help me avoid knee replacement?**

For many people with knee osteoarthritis pain, cooled radiofrequency is a way to reduce pain without surgery or to put surgery off. It treats the nerves that report pain rather than rebuilding the joint, so it does not correct deformity. In advanced grade 4 arthritis with joint deformity, a replacement may still be the right answer, and you will be told that plainly.

**Will radiofrequency ablation weaken my muscles?**

The procedure targets small sensory nerves that carry pain signals, chosen so that the nerves controlling the muscles you use to move are not treated. You may notice a patch of numbness or altered sensation over the treated area for a while. Report any new weakness to the team straight away.

## Prolotherapy in Hyderabad, for ligaments and tendons that no longer hold

Image-guided, under local anaesthetic, as day care — and chosen by what the diagnostic scan shows, not from a menu.

Book an appointment
Common questions

Prolotherapy is an injection treatment in which a natural irritant is placed into a slack or weakened ligament or tendon to restart the body’s own repair response. At Halcyon it is given under ultrasound guidance as a short course of small injections, as day care under local anaesthetic. Downtime is minimal, although some soreness for a day or two is normal.

### What is prolotherapy?

Prolotherapy, offered at Halcyon in Hyderabad, is a non-surgical injection treatment for ligaments and tendons that have become slack, overused or only partly healed. A natural irritant, most commonly a concentrated dextrose (sugar) solution, is injected where the structure attaches to bone or where it has weakened, to prompt the body to lay down repair tissue.
The aim is a ligament or tendon that holds again, rather than one that has simply been quietened.

### How prolotherapy works

Prolotherapy works by causing a small, controlled irritation in the injured tissue, which draws in the body’s natural healing response. Ligaments and tendons have a limited blood supply, so after repeated strain they often stop repairing fully and stay loose or painful.
The injected solution briefly stirs up that repair process in the precise spot the ultrasound shows is weak. Over a course of injections, the goal is firmer, better-organised tissue that supports the joint again. Because it relies on repair, improvement usually builds gradually over the course rather than appearing after the first injection.

### Which conditions prolotherapy helps

At Halcyon, prolotherapy is most often used for foot and ankle pain, knee pain and sports injuries — the heel, the Achilles, and a knee that gives way.
- Foot and ankle pain, including plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendon problems
- Knee pain where a ligament is lax or strained and the knee feels unstable
- Sports injuries to ligaments and tendons that have been overused or have only partly healed

### Who it suits, and who it does not

Prolotherapy usually suits people whose pain comes from a slack, overused or partly healed ligament or tendon, confirmed on ultrasound, and who have not recovered fully with rest, physiotherapy and simple measures. It suits these soft-tissue structures more than it suits a worn joint surface.
It is not the right choice when the pain comes mainly from worn cartilage, a trapped nerve or a complete tear that needs a different approach. In advanced grade 4 knee arthritis with deformity, a replacement may still be the right answer, and you will be told so plainly. An active infection or an allergy to any of the solutions used would also rule it out, and the consultant will check your medicines first.

### The procedure, step by step

Each session is short and done as day care at the Kukatpally centre, and most people are home within about two hours of arriving.
- The consultant takes your history and examines the joint.
- A diagnostic ultrasound in the same room shows which ligament or tendon is weak.
- If prolotherapy is right, the skin is cleaned and numbed with local anaesthetic.
- Under ultrasound guidance, small amounts of the solution are injected at the points that need it.
- You rest briefly and receive aftercare instructions.
- Further sessions in the course are booked; the consultant tells you how many are likely and how far apart.

### Recovery and aftercare

Downtime after prolotherapy is minimal. Some soreness, stiffness or swelling at the injection site for a day or two is normal and is part of the repair response.
You will be told which activities to reduce for a short while and when to return to exercise. Some anti-inflammatory painkillers may dampen the healing response, so ask the team which pain relief to use rather than choosing your own. A strengthening or physiotherapy programme alongside the course often helps the repaired tissue hold.

### Safety and side effects

Prolotherapy is generally well tolerated. The usual side effects are those of any injection: temporary pain, swelling, stiffness or bruising at the site. Rarely, infection or irritation of a nearby nerve can occur; ultrasound guidance helps the needle reach the intended tissue and avoid nearby nerves and vessels.
Contact the team if soreness is getting worse after the first few days rather than easing, and seek urgent care for fever, spreading redness or heat around the joint.

### Conditions it is used for

Each links to how that condition is assessed and treated at Halcyon.

- Foot & Ankle Pain
- Knee Pain
- Sports Injuries

### Questions about prolotherapy

**What is injected in prolotherapy?**

Prolotherapy uses a natural irritant, most commonly a concentrated dextrose (sugar) solution, often combined with a local anaesthetic. It is placed into the weakened ligament or tendon to trigger the body’s own repair response. At Halcyon the injections are given under ultrasound guidance, so the solution reaches the exact structure the scan has identified.

**How many prolotherapy sessions will I need?**

Prolotherapy is given as a short course of small injections rather than a single one, because repair builds up over time. The number of sessions depends on the structure treated, how long it has been injured and how you respond. The consultant will tell you how many are likely and how far apart they will be before you start.

**Is prolotherapy painful?**

The skin is numbed with local anaesthetic, and you stay awake throughout. You may feel pressure or a brief ache as the solution goes in. Some soreness for a day or two afterwards is normal, because the treatment works by stirring up a repair response. You will be told which pain relief to use while it settles.

**What is the difference between prolotherapy and regenerative medicine?**

Both aim to help tissue repair rather than just numb pain. Prolotherapy uses a natural irritant to restart healing in a slack ligament or tendon. Regenerative medicine at Halcyon uses a growth factor concentrate made from your own blood. Which suits you depends on the structure involved and what the ultrasound shows, and the consultant will explain the choice.

**Can prolotherapy help plantar fasciitis or Achilles pain?**

Heel pain from plantar fasciitis and pain from the Achilles tendon are among the problems prolotherapy is most often used for at Halcyon, alongside regenerative injections. The ultrasound shows how thickened or damaged the tissue is, and the treatment is placed precisely there. How much it helps varies, and the consultant will give you a realistic view.

**Can I walk and work after prolotherapy?**

Most people walk out after a session and return to ordinary daily activities quickly, as downtime is minimal. You may be advised to ease off heavy exercise or impact on that joint for a short time while the soreness settles. The consultant will tell you what to do and what to avoid before you leave.

## Nerve hydrodissection and nerve blocks in Hyderabad

Image-guided, under local anaesthetic, as day care — and chosen by what the diagnostic scan shows, not from a menu.

Book an appointment
Common questions

Nerve hydrodissection uses fluid, placed under ultrasound, to separate a trapped nerve from the tissue pressing on it, leaving the nerve itself intact. Nerve blocks are used both to treat a nerve that is firing and to prove where pain is coming from before anything else is done. At Halcyon both are done under local anaesthetic as day care, and you go home the same day.

### What are nerve hydrodissection and nerve blocks?

Nerve hydrodissection is a non-surgical procedure in which fluid is injected under ultrasound around a trapped (entrapped) nerve to separate it from the tissue that is pressing on or sticking to it. A nerve block is an injection placed on or beside a specific nerve to calm it, or to test whether it is the source of the pain.
At Halcyon in Hyderabad these form one pathway: freeing a nerve that is squeezed, and quietening one that is firing.

### How they work

Hydrodissection works by using a carefully placed volume of fluid to open up a space around a nerve that has become compressed or stuck. Healthy nerves glide as you move; when scar tissue, a thickened band or swollen tissue presses on one, it can cause pain, tingling or numbness. The fluid, usually saline and sometimes with local anaesthetic or dextrose, is watched on ultrasound as it lifts the tissue away. Relief often begins on the table.
A nerve block delivers medicine, usually a local anaesthetic and sometimes a steroid, to a precise point. Used diagnostically, a block that settles the pain is the strongest evidence available that the right structure has been found. Used as treatment, it can calm an irritated nerve so that movement and rehabilitation become possible.

### Which conditions they help

At Halcyon, hydrodissection and nerve blocks are most often used for these conditions. The named procedure depends on what the scan and examination show.
- Elbow, hand and wrist pain, such as carpal tunnel syndrome — nerve hydrodissection
- Sciatica — a transforaminal or epidural injection placed at the irritated nerve root
- Slipped disc pressing on a nerve root — an image-guided epidural injection
- Shoulder pain and frozen shoulder — a suprascapular nerve block, often with hydrodilatation
- Low back pain — a diagnostic or medial branch block to prove which structure is the source

### Who they suit, and who they do not

Hydrodissection usually suits people with symptoms of a trapped nerve — pain, pins and needles or numbness in the area that nerve supplies — where ultrasound shows the nerve being compressed. Nerve blocks suit people whose pain source needs confirming, or whose irritated nerve needs calming so that exercise and recovery can proceed.
They are not a substitute for urgent surgical assessment when there is severe or worsening weakness, or loss of bladder or bowel control. An active infection at the site, some bleeding problems, or poorly controlled diabetes may mean the procedure is delayed or changed, so tell the team about your health and medicines when you book.

### The procedure, step by step

Most of these procedures are completed in a single appointment at the Kukatpally centre, and most people are home within about two hours.
- The consultant takes your history and examines you, including nerve function.
- The nerve or structure is scanned with diagnostic ultrasound in the same room.
- If a procedure is right, the skin is cleaned and numbed with local anaesthetic.
- Under live imaging, a fine needle is guided to the nerve or to the chosen level of the spine.
- For hydrodissection, fluid is injected in stages to free the nerve along its course; for a block, the medicine is placed at the target.
- Your symptoms are checked, which for a diagnostic block helps decide the next step.
- You rest briefly, receive aftercare instructions and a review date, and go home.

### Recovery and aftercare

Most people walk out after hydrodissection or a nerve block and go about a normal day. The area may feel numb or heavy for a few hours while the local anaesthetic wears off, so take care with that limb and follow the advice you are given about driving.
Note how your pain changes over the following hours and days, especially after a diagnostic block, as this guides the plan. Gentle movement is usually encouraged; a stretching, splinting or exercise programme may be suggested to keep the nerve gliding freely.

### Safety and side effects

These procedures are generally well tolerated. Common effects are temporary numbness or weakness in the area supplied by the nerve, soreness and bruising at the needle site, and sometimes a short flare of symptoms. If a steroid is used, people with diabetes may notice a temporary rise in blood sugar.
Serious complications such as infection, bleeding or nerve injury are uncommon; ultrasound lets the consultant see the nerve and needle throughout. Seek urgent care for fever, spreading redness, new or worsening weakness, or loss of bladder or bowel control.

### Conditions it is used for

Each links to how that condition is assessed and treated at Halcyon.

- Elbow, Hand & Wrist
- Sciatica
- Slipped Disc
- Shoulder Pain
- Low Back Pain

### Questions about nerve hydrodissection & nerve blocks

**What is nerve hydrodissection?**

Nerve hydrodissection is an ultrasound-guided injection of fluid around a trapped nerve to separate it from the tissue pressing on it. The nerve is left intact and nothing is cut. It is often used for problems such as carpal tunnel syndrome, and relief often begins on the table. At Halcyon it is done under local anaesthetic as day care.

**Can carpal tunnel syndrome be treated without surgery?**

In many cases, yes. At Halcyon, carpal tunnel and similar wrist and elbow problems are usually treated with nerve hydrodissection or a regenerative injection rather than surgical release. Ultrasound shows where the median nerve is compressed, and fluid is used to free it. If the nerve is severely damaged or weakness is progressing, the consultant will tell you whether surgery should be considered.

**What is a diagnostic nerve block?**

A diagnostic nerve block is a small injection of local anaesthetic placed on one suspected structure. If the pain settles, that structure is the source and treatment follows from it; if it does not, the plan changes. In the low back and neck especially, this step is what stands between a diagnosis and a guess, and it comes before radiofrequency.

**Is a nerve block the same as an epidural injection?**

An epidural or transforaminal injection is one kind of nerve block, placed near the spinal nerve roots. At Halcyon it is the usual treatment for sciatica and for a slipped disc pressing on a nerve root, and it is placed under imaging at the level the scan and examination have identified, rather than across the whole area.

**How long does a nerve block last?**

It varies. The numbness from the local anaesthetic wears off within hours, but a treatment block can calm an irritated nerve for much longer, and some people need a repeat. How long relief lasts depends on the condition and what is causing it, and the consultant will give you a realistic answer for your case.

**Can I drive home after a nerve block?**

It depends on where the block is placed. A block in the leg, arm or spine can leave the limb numb or weak for a few hours, so it is safer to arrange for someone to drive you home. Ask the team when you book.

### At a glance

Guidance Ultrasound or other image guidance

Purpose Free a trapped nerve, or diagnose and treat a painful one

Anaesthesia Local anaesthetic; you stay awake

Hospital stay Day care, no admission

Surgery involved None; the nerve is left intact

## Dr. Dasyam Pallavi

Consultant – Pain Management. MBBS, DA, FIAPM, CIPS. Certified Interventional Pain Sonologist, World Institute of Pain (WIP), USA — consulting at Halcyon, Kukatpally.

Book an appointment
Both consultants

Dr. Dasyam Pallavi is a consultant in pain management at Halcyon Pain Management Centre in Kukatpally, Hyderabad. She holds the Certified Interventional Pain Sonologist (CIPS) credential awarded by the World Institute of Pain (WIP), USA, and is a Fellow of the Indian Academy of Pain Medicine (FIAPM). Her clinical work centres on ultrasound-guided pain interventions for musculoskeletal and nerve pain.

### International certification in ultrasound-guided pain interventions

Dr. Dasyam Pallavi holds the Certified Interventional Pain Sonologist (CIPS) credential awarded by the World Institute of Pain (WIP), USA.
CIPS is an international certification focused specifically on ultrasound-guided interventional pain procedures. It is not simply a course-completion certificate: the credential is awarded after successfully completing the World Institute of Pain’s structured examination process, which includes written, oral and practical, cadaver-based assessment.
The certification assesses a physician’s knowledge of the relevant anatomy and sonoanatomy, together with the practical application of ultrasound in interventional pain procedures. It is a specialised international credential held by a comparatively limited group of physicians who have completed the World Institute of Pain’s certification process.

### What CIPS means for patients

Many modern pain procedures can be performed under real-time ultrasound guidance, which lets the physician see the relevant nerves, muscles, tendons, joints and surrounding structures while performing the intervention.
A CIPS-certified physician has undergone a dedicated international assessment in the use of ultrasound for interventional pain procedures. This is particularly relevant to procedures involving peripheral nerves, joints and musculoskeletal structures.

### Fellowship in Pain Medicine

Dr. Pallavi is also a Fellow of the Indian Academy of Pain Medicine (FIAPM), reflecting dedicated training and professional development in the assessment and management of patients with acute and chronic pain conditions.

### Clinical areas of interest

Dr. Pallavi’s clinical work at Halcyon in Hyderabad includes:
- Ultrasound-guided pain interventions
- Musculoskeletal ultrasound
- Peripheral nerve interventions
- Radiofrequency procedures
- Joint and periarticular interventions
- Management of chronic musculoskeletal pain

## Dr. PSS Kiran

Consultant Radiologist – Musculoskeletal Imaging & Image Guidance. MBBS, MD (Radiodiagnosis), Fellowship in Pain Management — at Halcyon, Kukatpally.

Both consultants

Dr. PSS Kiran is the consultant radiologist for musculoskeletal imaging and image guidance at Halcyon Pain Management Centre in Kukatpally, Hyderabad. An MD Radiodiagnosis physician with additional fellowship training in pain management and musculoskeletal ultrasound, he focuses on the radiological evaluation of musculoskeletal and pain conditions — reading X-rays, MRI and ultrasound alongside the clinical picture.

### Musculoskeletal imaging in pain management

Dr. PSS Kiran is an MD Radiodiagnosis physician with additional fellowship training in Pain Management and Musculoskeletal Ultrasound. His clinical interests include musculoskeletal imaging, musculoskeletal ultrasound and the imaging evaluation of pain-related conditions.
His role at Halcyon focuses on the radiological evaluation of musculoskeletal and pain conditions, combining clinical information with relevant imaging such as X-rays, MRI and ultrasound.

### Why imaging matters in pain management

An abnormality seen on an MRI or X-ray does not always mean it is the actual source of a patient’s pain. Imaging findings need to be understood in the context of the patient’s symptoms and clinical examination.
Musculoskeletal ultrasound gives a real-time view of muscles, tendons, ligaments, joints and peripheral nerves, which helps assess many musculoskeletal conditions dynamically, as they move.

### An integrated clinical and imaging approach

At Halcyon, clinical assessment and musculoskeletal imaging are brought together to help identify the likely source of pain and to assist in appropriate treatment planning.
Dr. Kiran’s background in Radiodiagnosis, together with his additional training in Pain Management and Musculoskeletal Ultrasound, allows him to provide focused musculoskeletal ultrasound evaluation, imaging correlation and radiological assistance for image-guided pain procedures in collaboration with Dr. Dasyam Pallavi. His expertise complements her interventional pain practice, so the clinical and imaging information are considered together as part of an individualised approach to each patient.

- Musculoskeletal imaging
- Ultrasound evaluation of peripheral nerves
- Ultrasound assessment of muscles, tendons, ligaments and joints
- Correlation of MRI, X-ray and ultrasound findings in musculoskeletal pain
- Imaging evaluation of spinal and musculoskeletal pain conditions
- Radiological planning and image guidance for pain procedures
